caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No. It was carved.

On 16 October 1869 two men digging a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, hit a ten-foot stone body. Newell put a tent over it and charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute look. Three to five hundred people a day came.

The giant belonged to Newell's cousin, George Hull, a tobacconist who had lost an argument at a revival meeting about the giants named in Genesis 6:4. In 1868 he had a block of gypsum quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa — telling the workmen it was for a Lincoln monument — shipped it to a stonecutter in Chicago, and had it carved in his own likeness. A geologist told him hair does not petrify, so the giant is beardless. Sand and water, sulphuric acid and a board of steel knitting needles aged the surface. Cost: $2,600.

Geologists saw through it quickly. Yale's O. C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug": soluble gypsum, still carrying fresh tool marks. Andrew D. White asked the simpler question — why dig a well there, when a good spring already ran past the house? Hull confessed on 10 December 1869. In February 1870 a court declared both giants fake: his, and the plaster copy P. T. Barnum had made after his $50,000 offer was refused.

Still unresolved: whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter, knew what he was making.

Images: the giant photographed for Bain News Service in 1910; a lithograph titled "The Onondaga Giant"; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of the Fort Dodge gypsum quarry. All public domain.
